Khrushch, M., Worrell, E., Price, L., Martin, N. and Einstein, D. (1999). Carbon Emissions Reduction Potential in the US Chemicals and Pulp and Paper Industries by Applying CHP Technologies. Report LBNL-43739, Ernest Orlando Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, CA, June 1999. Also in Proceedings of the 1999 ACEEE Summer Study on Energy Efficiency in Industry, Saratoga Springs, NY, June 15-16, 1999. No DOI or URL printed.

Locators are the paper's printed page numbers (ACEEE proceedings pagination 1-14). The paper is mainly a sector-level CHP potential estimate, but it states the technology assumptions of its one pre-selected CHP system (natural-gas turbine + HRSG), which are loaded as two size classes (<=27 MW and >27 MW): electrical efficiency 33% (34% stated for >27 MW), total fuel utilization 80%, derived heat-to-power ratio and capacity factor (7,880 h/yr), 20-year lifetime, 10% discount rate, greenfield installed capex ($778/kW small, $605/kW large), fixed O&M ($23.4 and $19.5/kW) and variable O&M range (1.1-1.41 mills/kWh). _other-values.csv: the size-dependent efficiency and cost correlations, retrofit/brownfield costs, future-cost sensitivity values, carbon factors, grid efficiencies and the sector-level potentials. Not loaded: Table 2 scenario results cell by cell, Figure 2 cost curves (graph only), sector-level potentials as technology parameters. No flows file (no per-unit flows beyond efficiencies).

(1) No price year for any cost; costs come from a personal communication (Gerhardt 1998) and are not traceable. (2) The table of sensitivity results is captioned 'Table 2' but cited in the text as 'Table 1'. (3) The small-turbine efficiency relation gives about 35% at 27 MW, above the 34% stated for >27 MW (discontinuity); the study then uses 33% for all sizes. (4) Fixed O&M printed as '$/kW' without 'per year'. (5) Variable O&M range not split by size. (6) Table 2 labels one row 'CO2 savings (MtC)' (units of carbon, not CO2). (7) Report dated June 1999 though the task listing suggested c. 2000. (8) Efficiencies are LHV while MECS fuel data were converted from HHV with assumed latent-heat shares.
